400: Werther ran to the gate of the town.
The guards, who knew him, let him pass in silence.
The night was dark and stormy; it rained and snowed.
He reached his own door about eleven.
His servant, though he saw him come into the house without his hat, did not venture to say anything; and as he undressed his master he found that his clothes were wet.
His hat was found afterwards on the point of a rock overhanging the valley; and it is inconceivable how he could have climbed to the top on such a dark, tempestuous night without losing his life.
401: He went to bed and slept late.
The next morning his servant, called in to bring his coffee, found him writing.
He was adding to the letter to Charlotte what we set down here.
402: "For the last, last time I open these eyes.
Alas, they will see the sun no more.
It is covered by a thick, impenetrable cloud.
Yes, Nature, put on mourning: your child, your friend, your lover draws near his end.
This thought, Charlotte, is like nothing else; and yet it seems like a mysterious dream when I say it over — this is my last day!
The last!
Charlotte, no word can convey this thought.
The last!
Today I stand upright in all my strength; tomorrow, cold and stiff, I shall lie stretched on the ground.
To die! What is death?
We only dream when we talk about it.
I have seen many human beings die; but our feeble nature is so hemmed in that we have no clear conception of the beginning or the end of our existence.
At this moment I am my own — or rather I am yours, yours, my adored one! And the next moment we are parted, severed — perhaps for ever.
No, Charlotte, no!
How can I, how can you, be annihilated?
We exist.
What is annihilation?
A mere word, a meaningless sound that fixes no impression on the mind.
Dead, Charlotte! Laid in the cold earth, in the dark and narrow grave!
I had a friend once who was everything to me in my early youth.
She died.
I followed her hearse; I stood by her grave when the coffin was lowered.

And when I heard the creaking of the cords as they were loosened and drawn up, when the first shovelful of earth was thrown in and the coffin gave back a hollow sound, growing fainter and fainter until all was covered over, I threw myself on the ground.
My heart was smitten, grieved, shattered, torn — and I neither knew what had happened nor what was to happen to me.
Death! The grave! I do not understand the words.
Forgive, oh, forgive me!
Yesterday — ah, that day should have been the last of my life!
You angel! For the first time in my existence I felt rapture glow in my inmost soul.
She loves, she loves me!
Still there burns on my lips the sacred fire they took from yours.
New torrents of delight overwhelm my soul.
Forgive me, oh, forgive!
403: "I knew that I was dear to you; I saw it in your first entrancing look, knew it by the first pressure of your hand.
But when I was away from you, when I saw Albert at your side, my doubts and fears came back.
404: "Do you remember the flowers you sent me, when, at that crowded assembly, you could neither speak to me nor hold out your hand?
Half the night I was on my knees before those flowers, and I took them as pledges of your love; but those impressions grew fainter, and were at length effaced.
405: "Everything passes away; but a whole eternity could not put out the living flame your lips kindled yesterday, and which burns in me now.
These arms have held her waist, these lips have trembled on hers.
Yes, Charlotte, you are mine for ever.
406: "And what do they mean by saying Albert is your husband?
He may be so for this world; and in this world it is a sin to love you, to wish to tear you from his arms.
Yes, it is a crime, and I suffer the punishment for it — but I have had the full delight of my sin.
I have breathed in a balm that has revived my soul.
From this hour you are mine; yes, Charlotte, you are mine!
I go to my Father and to your Father.
I will pour out my sorrows before him, and he will comfort me until you come.
Then I will fly to meet you.
I will claim you, and stay in your eternal embrace, in the presence of the Almighty.
407: "I am not dreaming, I am not raving.
Drawing nearer to the grave, my perceptions grow clearer.
We shall exist; we shall see each other again; we shall see your mother.
I shall see her, and lay my inmost heart open to her.
408: About eleven o'clock Werther asked his servant whether Albert had come back.
He answered, "Yes," having seen him ride past; whereupon Werther sent him the following note, unsealed:
409: "Be so good as to lend me your pistols for a journey.
410: Charlotte had slept little during the night.
All her fears had come true in a way she could neither have foreseen nor avoided.
Her blood was boiling in her veins, and a thousand painful sensations tore at her pure heart.
Was it the ardour of Werther's passionate embraces that she felt in her breast?
Was it anger at his daring?
Was it the sad comparison of her present state with the days of innocence, tranquillity, and self-confidence that were gone?
How could she go to her husband and confess a scene she had no reason to conceal, and yet felt unwilling to avow?
They had kept silence toward each other so long — and was she to be the first to break it with so unexpected a disclosure?
She feared that the bare mention of Werther's visit would trouble him, and that her perfect candour would only deepen his distress.
She wished he could see her as she truly was, and judge her without prejudice; but did she want him to read her inmost soul?
On the other hand, could she deceive a man to whom all her thoughts had always been as clear as crystal, and from whom she had never hidden a feeling?
These reflections made her anxious and thoughtful.
Her mind still dwelt on Werther, who was now lost to her, whom she could not bring herself to give up, and for whom, she knew, nothing was left but despair if she were lost to him for ever.
411: The memory of that mysterious estrangement which had lately grown up between herself and Albert, and which she had never fully understood, was now painful to her beyond measure.
Even the prudent and the good have hesitated before now to explain their differences to one another, and have brooded in silence over imaginary grievances.
And so matters become so entangled that at the critical moment, when a calm explanation would have saved everyone, an understanding is no longer possible.

And so, if domestic confidence had been established between them earlier, if love and kind forbearance had opened and warmed their hearts toward each other, it might even yet not have been too late to save our friend.
412: But we must not forget one remarkable circumstance.
We may see from the character of Werther's correspondence that he had never made any secret of his anxious wish to leave this world.
He had often discussed the subject with Albert; and between Albert and Charlotte it had more than once been a topic of conversation.
Albert was so opposed to the very idea of such an act that, with an irritation unusual in him, he had more than once given Werther to understand that he doubted the seriousness of his threats.
He not only turned them into ridicule, but made Charlotte share his incredulity.
Her heart was thus set at rest whenever she felt inclined to take the melancholy subject seriously; though she never told her husband the apprehensions she sometimes felt.
413: Albert, on his return, was received by Charlotte with ill-concealed embarrassment.
He was out of humour himself; his business was unfinished, and he had just discovered that the neighbouring official he had to deal with was an obstinate and narrow-minded man.
Many things had happened to irritate him.
414: He asked whether anything had happened while he was away, and Charlotte answered hastily that Werther had been there the evening before.
He then asked for his letters, and was told that several packets had been left in his study.
415: The presence of the man she loved and honoured made a new impression on her heart.
The memory of his generosity, his kindness and his affection had calmed her agitation; a secret impulse urged her to follow him.
She took up her work and went to his study, as she often did.
He was busy opening and reading his letters.
Some of them seemed to contain disagreeable news.
She asked a few questions; he gave short answers, and sat down to write.
416: Several hours passed like this, and Charlotte's spirits grew more and more melancholy.
She felt how extremely difficult it would be, under any circumstances, to explain to her husband the weight that lay on her heart.
And her depression grew heavier every moment, in proportion to her efforts to hide her grief and conceal her tears.
417: The arrival of Werther's servant caused her the greatest embarrassment.
He gave Albert a note, which Albert handed coldly to his wife, saying at the same time, "Give him the pistols."
"I wish him a pleasant journey," he added, turning to the servant.
The words fell on Charlotte like a thunderbolt.
She rose from her seat half fainting, and hardly knowing what she was doing.
She walked mechanically toward the wall, took down the pistols with a trembling hand, slowly wiped the dust from them, and would have delayed longer had Albert not hurried her with an impatient look.
Then she gave the fatal weapons to the servant, unable to utter a word.
As soon as he had gone she folded up her work and went at once to her room, her heart overcome with the most fearful forebodings.

At one moment she was on the point of going to her husband, throwing herself at his feet, and telling him everything that had happened the evening before, so as to acknowledge her fault and explain her fears.
Then she saw that such a step would be useless, since she would certainly not be able to persuade Albert to go and see Werther.
Dinner was served; and a kind friend, whom she had persuaded to stay, helped to keep up the conversation, which was carried on by a kind of compulsion until the events of the morning were forgotten.
418: When the servant brought the pistols to Werther, he received them with transports of delight on hearing that Charlotte had given them to him with her own hand.
He ate some bread, drank some wine, sent his servant off to dinner, and then sat down to write as follows.
419: "They have been in your hands — you wiped the dust from them.
I kiss them a thousand times: you have touched them.
Yes, Heaven favours my design, and you, Charlotte, hand me the fatal instruments.
It was my wish to receive my death from your hands, and now my wish is granted.
You trembled when you gave him the pistols, but you sent me no farewell.
Wretched, wretched that I am — not one farewell!
How could you shut your heart against me in the very hour that makes you mine for ever?
Charlotte, ages cannot wear away the impression — I feel that you cannot hate the man who loves you so passionately."
420: After dinner he called his servant, told him to finish the packing, destroyed a great many papers, and then went out to pay some trifling debts.
He soon came home again, then went out once more in spite of the rain, walked for a while in the count's garden, and afterwards went further out into the country.
Toward evening he came back and took up his writing again.
421: "Wilhelm, I have looked for the last time on the mountains, the forests, and the sky.
And you, my dearest mother, forgive me!
I have settled all my affairs.
We shall meet again, and be happier than ever."
422: "I have repaid you badly, Albert; but you will forgive me.
I have disturbed the peace of your house.
I have sown distrust between you.
I will put an end to all this wretchedness.
And oh, that my death may make you happy!
Albert, Albert! Make that angel happy, and the blessing of Heaven be upon you."
423: He spent the rest of the evening arranging his papers; he tore up and burned a great many, and sealed others and addressed them to Wilhelm.
They contained some detached thoughts and maxims, a few of which I have read.
At ten o'clock he ordered his fire to be made up and a bottle of wine brought to him.
He then dismissed his servant, whose room, like the rooms of the rest of the household, was in another part of the house.
The servant lay down without undressing, so as to be ready the sooner for the journey in the morning, his master having told him the post-horses would be at the door before six.
424: All is silent around me, and my soul is calm.
I thank you, O God, for giving me strength and courage in these last moments.
I go to the window, my dearest of friends; and through the clouds, driven rapidly along at this moment by the furious wind, I see the stars that light the eternal heavens.
No, you will not fall, celestial bodies: the hand of the Almighty upholds you and me alike.
I have looked for the last time at the constellation of the Greater Bear.
It is my favourite star; for when I said goodnight to you at your door, Charlotte, and turned away, it always shone down on me.
With what rapture have I looked at it sometimes!
How often have I lifted my hands and begged it to witness my happiness! And even now —
But what object is there, Charlotte, that fails to call up your image before me?
Do you not surround me on every side? Have I not, like a child, treasured up every trifle your touch has made sacred?
425: "Your profile, which was so dear to me, I send back to you; and I beg you to keep it.
I have printed thousands of kisses on it, and a thousand times it has gladdened my heart as I left my house and came back to it.
426: "I have begged your father to protect my remains.
At the corner of the churchyard, looking out toward the fields, there are two lime-trees — there I wish to lie.
Your father can do this much for his friend, and no doubt he will.
But perhaps pious Christians will not wish their bodies to be buried beside the corpse of a poor, unhappy wretch like me.
Then let me be laid in some remote valley, or beside the highway, where the priest and the Levite may bless themselves as they pass my tomb, while the Samaritan sheds a tear for my fate.
427: "See, Charlotte, I do not shudder to take the cold and fatal cup from which I shall drink the draught of death.
Your hand holds it out to me, and I do not tremble.
All, all is now concluded: the wishes and the hopes of my life are fulfilled.
With a cold, unflinching hand I knock at the brazen gates of Death.
Oh, that I had been granted the bliss of dying for you! How gladly I would have sacrificed myself for you, Charlotte!
And if I could give peace and joy back to your heart, with what resolution, with what joy, would I meet my fate!
But it is the lot of only a chosen few to shed their blood for their friends, and by their death to multiply a thousandfold the happiness of those who love them.
428: "I wish, Charlotte, to be buried in the clothes I am wearing now: your touch has made them sacred.
I have begged this favour of your father.
My spirit soars above my grave.
I do not wish my pockets to be searched.
The knot of pink ribbon you wore at your breast the first time I saw you, surrounded by the children —
Oh, kiss them a thousand times for me, and tell them the fate of their unhappy friend.
I think I see them playing around me.
How warmly I have been attached to you, Charlotte!
Since the first hour I saw you, how impossible I have found it to leave you.
This ribbon must be buried with me: it was a present from you on my birthday.
Little did I think then that I should travel this road.
429: "They are loaded — the clock strikes twelve.
430: A neighbour saw the flash and heard the report of the pistol; but as everything stayed quiet afterwards, he thought no more of it.
431: In the morning, at six o'clock, the servant went into Werther's room with a candle.
He found his master stretched on the floor, weltering in his blood, the pistols at his side.
He called to him, he took him in his arms, but got no answer.
Life was not yet quite extinct.
The servant ran for a surgeon, and then went to fetch Albert.
Charlotte heard the ringing of the bell, and a cold shudder seized her.
She woke her husband, and they both got up.
The servant, bathed in tears, faltered out the dreadful news.
Charlotte fell senseless at Albert's feet.
432: When the surgeon came to the unfortunate Werther, he was still lying on the floor; his pulse beat, but his limbs were cold.
The bullet, entering the forehead over the right eye, had gone through the skull.
A vein was opened in his right arm; the blood came, and he still went on breathing.
433: From the blood that had run down the chair, it could be inferred that he had done the act sitting at his desk, and had afterwards fallen to the floor.
He was found lying on his back near the window.
434: The house, the neighbourhood, and the whole town were immediately in commotion.
They had laid Werther on the bed; his head was bound up, and the pallor of death was on his face.
His limbs were motionless, but he still breathed — at times strongly, then more weakly; his death was expected at any moment.
435: He had drunk only one glass of the wine.
"Emilia Galotti" lay open on his desk.
436: I shall say nothing of Albert's distress, or of Charlotte's grief.
437: The old steward hurried to the house the moment he heard the news; he embraced his dying friend in a flood of tears.
His eldest boys soon followed him on foot.
In speechless sorrow they threw themselves on their knees by the bedside and kissed his hands and his face.
The eldest, who was his favourite, hung over him until he died, and even then had to be taken away by force.
At twelve o'clock Werther breathed his last.
The steward's presence, and the precautions he had taken, prevented any disturbance; and that night, at eleven, he had the body buried in the place Werther had chosen for himself.
438: The steward and his sons followed the body to the grave.
Albert was unable to go with them.
The body was carried by labourers.
